prize_parts.citation: For an encyclopedic, visionary Romanian-language prose and poetry in which memory, the body and dream are built into a cosmological architecture that renews the European tradition of inward and fantastic narrative.

statement.case_for: Cărtărescu remains my first choice on the common criteria. The voice is highly distinctive: dense, patterned prose in which the body, memory and dream become one metaphysical project. As far as public knowledge shows, the formal ambition is sustained at large scale in Blinding (the opening volume of the Orbitor trilogy) and Solenoid, and the imaginative and intellectual depth does not depend on topical significance. The oeuvre also seems to extend beyond the long novels into poetry and shorter prose, so a whole-oeuvre judgment is possible. The late large works appear to extend the early project rather than repeat it. The single-writer attribution is clean and a citation can be precise. The Nobel prize honours a whole body of work rather than one book, and in this shortlist his seems the most coherent and consolidated body of work. I make this case without relying on nationality, language or fame as a stand-in for merit.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that my judgment of the prose rests heavily on translation, and the density and long-sentence control of the Romanian original may not carry over fully. Coverage of the poetry and early work in translation is thinner than for the major novels. The very long, self-referential novels may also be uneven over their length, or may limit significance beyond readers of ambitious fiction. I cannot verify any of this by independent reading. If the committee concluded that the late novels excessively repeat the early architecture, the case for B024 would weaken, and Yan Lianke's formal range or Anne Carson's formal invention would be the next comparisons to test.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first on voice, form and depth, but warns that translation may flatten the Romanian prose texture and that the late novels may be uneven or excessive in length. She also notes that Murnane's narrow range may limit his claim to wide significance, and that Yan Lianke's case must rest on the texts rather than on political suppression.
responses.response: I agree on the translation and length caveats, and I treat them as real uncertainties about B024, not as settled strengths. Her point about Murnane matches my own placing of him sixth: his formal rigour is clear, but the intensity of the achievement seems greater than its breadth. I also agree that Yan Lianke should be argued from narrative form, such as the mythic and grotesque modes and his stated poetics of mythorealism, and not from the circumstances of publication. That is why I keep him as my first alternative but not above Cărtărescu, since the Chinese register is hard for me to judge through translation.

responses.point: Carlberg also ranks Cărtărescu first for the coherence and scale of his imaginative architecture. She questions whether Carson's achievement is sustained over many volumes or concentrated in a few landmark books, and how her ironic and formally radical work fits the will's reference to an idealistic tendency.
responses.response: I share her question about Carson's sustained quality. I have said that some of Carson's work is fragmentary or occasional, which complicates a whole-oeuvre judgment, and Autobiography of Red and Nox may weigh more than the many shorter pieces. I would qualify the worry about idealistic tendency, though. The will's wording is open to interpretation, and I would not exclude a writer on formal or ironic grounds alone without a shared reading of it. I therefore keep Carson as a serious alternative but not the preferred choice. The case for Cărtărescu rests on a larger, more continuous body of work.

responses.point: Palm ranks Alexis Wright second, arguing that Carpentaria and The Swan Book reshape the novel through Indigenous oral forms and ecological time, with imaginative depth beyond topical significance. She acknowledges that the oeuvre is modest in size and that political significance must not stand in for merit.
responses.response: I accept that the formal and linguistic case for Wright is substantial and not merely topical, and I appreciate her stress that the argument must rest on form. I ranked Wright fifth because the major novelistic corpus is small, and that bears on the criterion of sustained quality across a body of work. Her nonfiction and recent work may widen that corpus, but my knowledge of them is less detailed. The comparison with Cărtărescu therefore turns on whether a compact corpus of two major novels can carry a whole-oeuvre citation as well as a longer, still-developing one. For now I think it carries less, but I am open to being persuaded by closer discussion of the later work.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Adonis second for reshaping modern Arabic poetic language and notes that timing is delicate because of his age. He also stresses that Cărtărescu's citation should not be framed as national symbolism.
responses.response: I agree that the Cărtărescu citation should be framed in terms of literary form and imagination and not national symbolism, and my proposed wording does so. On Adonis, I regard age and timing as irrelevant to literary merit, so I would not weigh them. My reservation is different: the main influence of his formal and linguistic achievement belongs to earlier decades and operates inside Arabic poetry, where translation loss is greatest, so I cannot judge recent sustained quality well. That is why I placed him seventh. If colleagues who can speak to the Arabic originals argue for his sustained recent work, I would reconsider.

uncertainties: How far the density and long-sentence control of Cărtărescu's Romanian prose is conveyed in translation, and whether the late very long novels are uneven.
Coverage of Cărtărescu's poetry and early work in translation is incomplete, so the whole-oeuvre judgment relies on the major novels.
How the will's reference to an idealistic tendency should be read when comparing formally radical or ironic writers such as Carson.
Whether Yan Lianke's sustained quality can be judged reliably given uneven translation and restricted circulation of some works.
How much weight should go to a compact corpus (Wright) compared with a longer, still-developing one.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. I serve on the committee with the other listed members, but the profile shows no personal or institutional connection to any shortlisted writer. My own practice as a novelist is context, not a basis for favouring any candidate.
